newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Marcos lawyers slam U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Marcos lawyers slam U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Lawyers for Imelda Marcos on Tuesday described an attempt to enforce a U.S. court order instructing her family to pay $1.2 billion damages to victims of human rights abuses as "judicial imperialism".

"Whatever happened to Philippine independence and sovereignty?" the lawyers for the former first lady said in a petition asking a court in Manila's Makati business district not to recognise the U.S. ruling.
A jury in Hawaii awarded the judgment in 1994 in a class suit filed by about 9,500 alleged victims of human rights abuses during the rule of late president Ferdinand Marcos.
A U.S. appeals court upheld the award in December.
The victims' lawyers last month asked the Makati court to enforce the U.S. verdict as "a valid foreign judgment".
They also asked for authority to question Mrs Marcos on the extent and whereabouts of her family assets.
Marcos lawyers contended the alleged violations occurred in the Philippines and involved Filipinos, and said enforcing the U.S. ruling would undermine the Constitution and judicial system.
"This case is a case of U.S. judicial imperialism," one of the lawyers, Reynaldo Dario, said.
Dozens of Marcos supporters picketed the court during the hearing and shouted at human rights lawyer Rene Saguisag as she left.
"You're a Filipino, not a foreigner," one protester shouted.
American human rights lawyer Robert Swift told reporters the victims remained open to a compromise settlement if the Marcoses made "a reasonable offer".
The Philippine government has seized Marcos assets and accuses the family of looting up to $5 billion from the economy during their 20-year rule.
Ferdinand Marcos was ousted in a 1986 popular revolt and died in Hawaii in 1989.
